title: Early somatic mosaicism is a rare cause of long-QT syndrome

venue.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

abstract: 1.5 encoded by SCN5A, NM_000335:c.5284G > T predicting p.(V1762L), but read depth was insufficient to be diagnostic. Exome sequencing of the trio confirmed read ratios inconsistent with Mendelian inheritance only in the proband. Genotyping of single circulating leukocytes demonstrated the mutation in the genomes of 8% of patient cells, and RNA sequencing of cardiac tissue from the infant confirmed the expression of the mutant allele at mosaic ratios. Heterologous expression of the mutant channel revealed significantly delayed sodium current with a dominant negative effect. To investigate the mechanism by which mosaicism might cause arrhythmia, we built a finite element simulation model incorporating Purkinje fiber activation. This model confirmed the pathogenic consequences of cardiac cellular mosaicism and, under the presenting conditions of this case, recapitulated 2:1 AV block and arrhythmia. To investigate the extent to which mosaicism might explain undiagnosed arrhythmia, we studied 7,500 affected probands undergoing commercial gene-panel testing. Four individuals with pathogenic variants arising from early somatic mutation events were found. Here we establish cardiac mosaicism as a causal mechanism for LQTS and present methods by which the general phenomenon, likely to be relevant for all genetic diseases, can be detected through single-cell analysis and next-generation sequencing.

stewardship.abstract: Somatic mosaicism, the occurrence and propagation of genetic variation in cell lineages after fertilization, is increasingly recognized to play a causal role in a variety of human diseases. We investigated the case of life-threatening arrhythmia in a 10-day-old infant with long QT syndrome (LQTS). Rapid genome sequencing suggested a variant in the sodium channel Na<sub>V</sub>1.5 encoded by SCN5A, NM_000335:c.5284G > T predicting p.(V1762L), but read depth was insufficient to be diagnostic. Exome sequencing of the trio confirmed read ratios inconsistent with Mendelian inheritance only in the proband. Genotyping of single circulating leukocytes demonstrated the mutation in the genomes of 8% of patient cells, and RNA sequencing of cardiac tissue from the infant confirmed the expression of the mutant allele at mosaic ratios. Heterologous expression of the mutant channel revealed significantly delayed sodium current with a dominant negative effect. To investigate the mechanism by which mosaicism might cause arrhythmia, we built a finite element simulation model incorporating Purkinje fiber activation. This model confirmed the pathogenic consequences of cardiac cellular mosaicism and, under the presenting conditions of this case, recapitulated 2:1 AV block and arrhythmia. To investigate the extent to which mosaicism might explain undiagnosed arrhythmia, we studied 7,500 affected probands undergoing commercial gene-panel testing. Four individuals with pathogenic variants arising from early somatic mutation events were found. Here we establish cardiac mosaicism as a causal mechanism for LQTS and present methods by which the general phenomenon, likely to be relevant for all genetic diseases, can be detected through single-cell analysis and next-generation sequencing.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2016 PNAS article has accumulated 51 citations and sits in the top 10% of cited papers for its field and year, indicating clear scholarly uptake. Its influence is visible not only in later cardiovascular genetics papers but also in reviews and preprints that use it as a reference point for somatic mosaicism in inherited arrhythmia.

Full narrative

Priest and colleagues addressed a clinically important question in long-QT syndrome: whether an apparently Mendelian cardiac disorder could instead arise from early somatic mosaicism. By combining rapid genome sequencing, exome analysis, single-cell leukocyte genotyping, and RNA sequencing of cardiac tissue, the study provided a strong mechanistic case that a pathogenic SCN5A variant was present in only a subset of the patient’s cells and was expressed in mosaic form in the heart. The work helped establish mosaicism as a real, if uncommon, explanation for life-threatening arrhythmia in infancy.

The paper’s downstream footprint is concentrated in cardiovascular electrophysiology, genomics, and rare-disease genetics. Its citing literature is anchored by research articles, but it also appears in reviews and preprints, suggesting that it has served both as primary evidence and as a framing example for later discussion of mosaic variation in diagnosis and interpretation. Recent citing works show continued relevance in 2024–2026, including papers on computational cardiology, cardiac digital twins, sudden death phenotyping, and the clinical relevance of mosaic variants detected by exome sequencing.

This pattern points to a work that is not merely well cited, but conceptually generative: it helped normalize the idea that postzygotic variation can matter in inherited cardiac disease and can be detected through careful integration of sequencing and tissue-based validation. That interpretive reach is reinforced by its reuse in 52 downstream works and by its appearance in review literature, where it functions as a reference point for broader syntheses of somatic variation and arrhythmia biology.

The surrounding record shows limited public-discourse activity in the sources captured here, so the most visible impact is scholarly rather than media-driven. The article is also backed by substantial NIH and NHLBI funding, consistent with a translational genomics study that bridged clinical observation, sequencing technology, and cardiac electrophysiology. Overall, the evidence shows steady and durable academic influence, with especially strong resonance in work on mosaicism, rare disease genetics, and precision cardiology.
